intro.h1: Plan your Wi-Fi mesh on your floor plan
intro.p: Planejador WiFi shows where the signal reaches before you buy a router: draw the walls, place the router and mesh nodes, and see the coverage on 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. Free, no sign-up, and your projects stay in your browser.

guide.howToSteps:
• Click Start my project (or New project) and give it a name. The sheet opens at 16 × 12 m; change its size under File › Plan and scale if needed.
  • If you have the floor plan as a photo or an image, load it under File › Plan and scale and set the scale with Measure.
  • With the Wall tool, click each corner: walls follow one another, and clicking the first point closes the room. Rectangle draws a whole room at once. Pick the material; doors and windows are walls too, made of wood or glass.
  • With Router, place the main router where the ISP modem is, then the other nodes.
  • Switch between 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz and look at the heat map. Green is excellent signal; red is no usable signal.
  • Use Suggest a spot to find where one more node helps most, and File › Export JSON to keep the project.
guide.wallsTitle: How much each wall takes from the signal
guide.wallsText: Every wall the signal crosses adds a loss in decibels (dB). Each 10 dB cuts the received power to one tenth, so two or three brick walls already make a difference. The values below are the averages the planner uses; real loss depends on thickness, moisture and steel reinforcement.
guide.signalText: Wi-Fi signal is measured in dBm and is always negative: the closer to zero, the better.
guide.bandsText:
2.4 GHz reaches farther and goes through walls better, but it is slow and shared with your neighbors. Good for smart-home devices and far corners.

5 GHz is the everyday balance: much faster, with medium range. Check the map on this band first.

6 GHz, found on Wi-Fi 6E and tri-band Wi-Fi 7 routers, is the fastest and least crowded, but loses more at every wall. It shines in the router's own room and on the link between mesh nodes.
signalUse: 4K streaming, online gaming and the full speed of your plan.
Stable HD video and video calls. The target for rooms you use.
Browsing and messaging work; video may stutter.

faq.a: It is an estimate with a typical error of 8 dB either way. Use it to compare placements and decide how many nodes to buy. After installing, confirm with a Wi-Fi analyzer app on your phone.

faq.q: How many mesh nodes do I need?
faq.a: As a rule of thumb, one node per 80 to 120 m² (860 to 1,300 sq ft) in a brick house, and one per floor in multi-story homes. Concrete walls, slabs and long houses need more. Draw your plan and use Suggest a spot to see whether another node pays off.

faq.q: Where should I put the main router?
faq.a: As close to the center of the house as possible, about 1 meter (3 ft) off the floor, away from fridges, mirrors and metal cabinets. If the modem sits in a corner, run a network cable to a central spot or put a mesh node there.

faq.q: Is a Wi-Fi 7 mesh with 6 GHz worth it?
faq.a: The 6 GHz band is fast and uncrowded but goes through walls poorly. It is most useful for the link between nodes and for devices in the same room. For internet plans up to 1 Gbps, a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh is usually enough.
Wired whenever you can: speed does not drop and nodes can sit farther apart. Wirelessly, aim for −60 to −70 dBm between nodes. Below that, devices connected to the far node get much slower.
Only in your browser, in the device's local storage. Nothing is sent to a server. To keep a copy or open it on another computer, use File and then Export JSON.

router.title: Where to Put Your Wi-Fi Router at Home | Planejador WiFi
router.description: The best spot for a router is the middle of the home, 1 to 2 m off the floor and away from metal. See how much each wall cuts its range and what to do if the modem is in a corner.
router.h1: Where should you put your Wi-Fi router?
router.answer:
Put the router in the middle of your home, 1 to 2 meters off the floor, out in the open and away from metal, mirrors and the fridge. The best spot is the one with the fewest walls between the router and the rooms where you use the internet most.

Walls matter more than distance. In the Planejador WiFi model, good 5 GHz signal reaches about {range.b5} m with nothing in the way, {range.b5.tijolo} m through one brick wall and {range.b5.tijolo.2} m through two.

If your ISP’s modem sits in a corner, bring the router to the middle with a network cable or use a mesh system. In a two-story home the floor slab takes {db.slab.b5} dB off the 5 GHz signal, and one node per floor usually solves it.

sections.q: Why is the middle of the home the best spot?
sections.html:
A router sends its signal out in every direction, roughly evenly. From a corner, half of it goes to the street or the neighbors, and the room on the far side gets both the longest distance and the most walls.

From the middle, the distance to the farthest room is cut in half, and most rooms end up one or two walls away. “Middle” means the middle of where you use the internet: if the office and the living room are on one side and the garage on the other, move the router toward the side that matters.

sections.q: What matters more: distance or walls?
sections.html:
Walls. Each wall takes off a fixed number of decibels, and the signal lost that way is worth many meters of distance. In the planner’s model, one brick wall divides the distance at which 5 GHz signal stays good by {factor.b5.tijolo}; a concrete wall divides it by {factor.b5.concreto}.

  • No walls: good signal up to about {range.b5} m on 5 GHz and {range.b24} m on 2.4 GHz.
  • One brick wall: {range.b5.tijolo} m on 5 GHz and {range.b24.tijolo} m on 2.4 GHz.
  • Two brick walls: {range.b5.tijolo.2} m on 5 GHz and {range.b24.tijolo.2} m on 2.4 GHz.
  • One concrete wall or pillar: {range.b5.concreto} m on 5 GHz.

So when you pick a spot, count the walls between the router and each room before you measure the distance. “Good signal” here means {level.1} dBm or better, enough for HD video and video calls.

sections.q: How high should the router be?
sections.html: Between 1 and 2 meters off the floor, on a shelf or mounted on the wall, with open space around it. On the floor, the signal has to get through furniture and people before it reaches your devices. On a high shelf, it clears most of the furniture.

sections.q: What should you keep away from the router?
sections.html:
• Metal, mirrors and the fridge: they reflect and block the signal. The model counts {db.metal.b5} dB on 5 GHz for them; a concrete wall counts {db.concreto.b5} dB.
  • Aquariums and water tanks: water absorbs Wi-Fi frequencies well.
  • Microwave ovens: they run near 2.4 GHz and disturb that band while they are on.
  • Behind the TV or inside an AV cabinet: TVs have metal backs, and the cabinet surrounds the router with electronics.

sections.q: What if the ISP’s modem is in a corner?
sections.html:
The modem goes where the ISP’s cable or fiber comes in, and that is rarely the middle of the home. There are three ways out, from simplest to most complete:

  1. A network cable to the middle: run a network cable (Cat 5e or Cat 6) from the modem to a router in the middle of the home, and turn off the modem’s Wi-Fi so two networks don’t compete for the same space.
  2. A mesh system: the main node sits next to the modem, connected by cable, and a second node goes near the middle or the far side. The nodes talk to each other wirelessly or, better, over a cable.
  3. Move the ISP’s outlet: ask the technician to install the modem somewhere more central on the next visit.

sections.q: Where should it go in a two-story home?
sections.html:
The slab between floors takes {db.slab.b5} dB off the 5 GHz signal and {db.slab.b24} dB off 2.4 GHz, more than most walls. With the router downstairs, good 5 GHz signal reaches about {range.b5.slab} m in a straight line upstairs, before counting any walls up there.

If one floor gets much more use, put the router there. If both do, a high spot in the middle of the ground floor (near the ceiling, on a tall bookcase) helps, but the most reliable setup is one mesh node per floor, ideally one above the other and, if you can, wired together.

sections.q: How do you know the spot works?
sections.html:
Measure the signal strength, in dBm, in the rooms you use most. Aim for {level.1} dBm or better; {level.0} dBm or better is excellent. Below {level.2} dBm the connection gets slow and unstable.

  • Android: a Wi-Fi analyzer app shows the value in dBm.
  • iPhone: install Apple’s AirPort Utility app and turn on “Wi-Fi Scanner” under Settings › AirPort Utility.
  • Mac: hold Option and click the Wi-Fi icon; the value shows as RSSI.

Before you drill a hole or buy cable, try the spots in the planner: draw your floor plan, move the router around and compare the signal map for each option.

faq.q: Can I hide the router in a cabinet?
faq.a: You can, but it loses range. A wooden door takes {db.madeira.b5} dB off 5 GHz and a metal cabinet or rack {db.metal.b5} dB, which can cost a whole room of coverage. If you need to hide it, use open shelving or leave the door open.

faq.q: Should the router’s antennas point up?
faq.a: On most routers, yes. External antennas spread the signal more to the sides than up and down, so upright antennas cover the same floor best. In a two-story home, tilting one antenna often helps the floor above. Models with internal antennas should stand the way they come in the box.

faq.q: Is one router enough, or do I need mesh?
faq.a: One router is usually enough when every room you use is at most two brick walls away from it: up to about {range.b5.tijolo.2} m with two walls in the way, on 5 GHz. Larger, long or two-story homes usually need more than one access point. The planner shows this on your own floor plan.
